paragraphs.simple: There is no real coffee or tea because of the war. The mothers drink hot water with herbs, but they still call it coffee.

paragraphs.mainIdea: The Free Danes is an illegal newspaper Peter secretly delivers; Mama burns it after reading. It reports Danish sabotage against the Nazis.
paragraphs.simple: Peter secretly brings them a banned newspaper, and Mama burns it after reading. It tells how Danes damage Nazi factories and trains.

paragraphs.context: It is important to be one of the crowd, always.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. Rosen warns the girls to always blend into the crowd. They must never give the soldiers a reason to notice or remember their faces.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Rosen tells the girls to stay unnoticed among many people. The soldiers must never have a reason to remember what they look like.

paragraphs.context: King Christian was a real human being, a man
paragraphs.mainIdea: Unlike storybook kings, King Christian is a real, kind man. Each morning he rides his horse Jubilee alone through Copenhagen, greeting his people.
paragraphs.simple: King Christian is not like fairy-tale kings. He is a real, kind man. Each morning he rides his horse alone through the city, greeting the people.

paragraphs.context: The boy looked right at the soldier, and he
paragraphs.mainIdea: When the soldier asks where the king's bodyguard is, the boy answers proudly: all of Denmark protects the king.
paragraphs.simple: The soldier asks where the king's guard is. The boy answers that every person in Denmark guards and protects the king.

paragraphs.context: It was her tall, beautiful sister who had died
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lise, Annemarie's beautiful older sister, died in an accident two weeks before her wedding. Her unworn wedding dress lies folded in the bedroom trunk.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie's older sister Lise died just before her wedding. Her wedding dress was never worn. It lies folded in a trunk in the bedroom.

paragraphs.context: because electricity was rationed now. At night they used

paragraphs.simple: There is no fuel because of the war, and electricity is limited. They burn coal in a small stove and use candles for light at night.

paragraphs.mainIdea: Copenhagen has a curfew: no one may go out after eight o'clock. Peter's nighttime visit is very dangerous, yet Annemarie is happy to see him.
paragraphs.simple: No one in Copenhagen may go out after eight at night. Peter's late visit is very dangerous, but Annemarie is happy to see him.

paragraphs.context: It is their way of tormenting. For some reason,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Peter explains that the Nazis torment Jewish people on purpose. It has already happened in other countries, and now it is starting in Denmark.
paragraphs.simple: Peter says the Nazis hurt Jewish people on purpose. They did this in other countries first. Now they are starting to do it in Denmark.

paragraphs.mainIdea: Annemarie recognized the strange fishing words from Papa's phone call and wondered what they really meant, since Henrik fished every day in any weather.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie had heard those words on the telephone. She did not know their secret meaning. But Henrik fished every day, rain or shine, so they had to mean something else.

paragraphs.context: tonight your Great-aunt Birte will be resting in the living
paragraphs.mainIdea: Henrik said their very old Great-aunt Birte had died; that night she would rest in her casket in the living room, by old custom.
paragraphs.simple: Henrik said the death was sad but not too sad; she was very old. That night Great-aunt Birte would rest in her casket in the living room, following the old custom.

paragraphs.context: And Annemarie was quite, quite certain, though she said nothing.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annemarie was quite certain there was no Great-aunt Birte — she knew all her mother's family stories — though she said nothing.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie knew her mother's family well. She remembered every aunt and uncle from the stories. She was sure no Great-aunt Birte existed. But she said nothing.

paragraphs.context: it is much easier to be brave if you do not
paragraphs.mainIdea: Henrik said it is easier to be brave when you do not know everything; Mama did not know everything either — they knew only what they needed to know.
paragraphs.simple: Henrik said knowing less makes bravery easier. Mama did not know the whole secret either. They each knew only what they needed to know.

paragraphs.context: If she had known everything, it would not have been
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annemarie had answered the soldier bravely because she did not know the Germans would take the Jews; full knowledge would have made it harder.
paragraphs.simple: That day Annemarie answered the soldier even though she was frightened, because she did not know the Germans would take the Jews. Full knowledge would have made bravery much harder.

paragraphs.context: to help you to be brave, because we love you.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Henrik admitted there was no Great-aunt Birte; he and Mama had lied to help Annemarie be brave, because they loved her, and he asked her forgiveness.
paragraphs.simple: Henrik explained the lie. He and Mama lied to help her be brave, because they loved her. Then he asked: would she forgive them?

paragraphs.context: She understood that she was protecting Ellen the way her
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annemarie said nothing, realizing she was now lying to Ellen too — protecting her best friend the way Mama had protected her.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie could have told Ellen the truth. But she stayed silent. She was keeping Ellen safe by letting her believe the lie, just as Mama had kept her safe.

paragraphs.context: In that moment, with that look, they became equals.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mama called the visitors 'friends of Great-aunt Birte'; Annemarie knew Mama was lying, Mama knew she knew, and with that long look they became equals.
paragraphs.simple: Mama lied about the visitors again. Each knew the other knew. They held each other's gaze in silence, and in that moment mother and daughter became equals.

paragraphs.context: these people had nothing to talk about. They couldn't speak of
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annemarie realized these silent visitors had nothing to talk about: unlike at Lise's funeral, there had never been a Great-aunt Birte to remember.
paragraphs.simple: At Lise's funeral, friends had talked of happy memories. But these people sat silent. They could not share memories of Great-aunt Birte, because she had never existed.

paragraphs.context: "Good. Here they come," he said in a low, relieved
paragraphs.mainIdea: Looking into the darkness, Henrik said with relief, 'Here they come,' and asked Ellen to come with him.
paragraphs.simple: Henrik stared into the dark yard. Then he spoke in a low, happy voice. The people were coming. He told Ellen to go with him.

paragraphs.context: she returned—held tightly, like a little girl, her bare legs
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ellen returned held tightly against her father's chest, her bare legs dangling, with her mother beside them — her parents had come.
paragraphs.simple: Ellen came back inside. Her father held her tight against his chest like a small child. Her bare legs dangled. Her mother walked beside them.

paragraphs.context: Now she knew for certain what Uncle Henrik had meant
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annemarie now understands Henrik's words from the barn: it is easier to be brave when you know nothing about the danger.
paragraphs.simple: She finally gets what Henrik meant. A person can be brave more easily if she does not know what is really happening.

paragraphs.context: It seems odd to me that you have closed this coffin up so tightly.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The officer says it is strange that the casket is shut so tight, since their custom is to look at the dead person's face.
paragraphs.simple: He tells Mama it is odd the box is closed. He says their people always look at the dead one last time, so he wants it opened.

paragraphs.context: Surely typhus germs wouldn't linger in a dead person!
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mama pretends to agree, saying the doctor warned the casket must stay shut because typhus germs might still be dangerous.
paragraphs.simple: She quickly says the doctor told them to keep it closed: Aunt Birte died of typhus, and the germs could still hurt people. Still, she wants one last look.

paragraphs.context: How could anyone number them one by one, as the psalm said?
paragraphs.mainIdea: The psalm says God counts the stars one by one, and Annemarie wonders how anyone could do that when there are so many stars.
paragraphs.simple: She hears that God counts every star. Looking at the huge night sky, she wonders how anyone could count so many.

paragraphs.context: the pounding on the door, and then the heavy, frighteningly familiar staccato of boots
paragraphs.mainIdea: The soldiers' arrival feels like a nightmare coming again: pounding on the door, then the heavy beat of boots she knows too well.
paragraphs.simple: She hears the door pound and the loud steps of boots on the kitchen floor. She has heard those frightening steps before. The woman with the baby starts to cry.

paragraphs.context: "My Great-aunt Birte," she lied, in a firm voice.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Everyone watches her, and Annemarie understands the officer is asking her. She answers with a firm lie: her great-aunt Birte died.
paragraphs.simple: No one speaks. All eyes are on Annemarie. She knows she must answer. She swallows and says in a steady voice that her Great-aunt Birte died.

paragraphs.context: It was one more time, Annemarie realized, when they protected one another
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annemarie understands their rule: they protect each other by not asking or telling, so no one has dangerous knowledge to fear or share.
paragraphs.simple: She sees it is their way: Mr. Rosen does not ask what the packet is, and Peter does not tell. Not knowing keeps them safer.

paragraphs.context: she had heard Peter Neilsen call her mother by her first name
paragraphs.mainIdea: For the first time, Peter calls her mother 'Inge' instead of 'Mrs. Johansen', as if he has stepped into the world of adults.
paragraphs.simple: Before, he always said 'Mrs. Johansen'. Now he uses her first name, like a grown-up speaking to another grown-up. He has left his young days behind.

paragraphs.context: those sources of pride—the candlesticks, the books, the daydreams of theater
paragraphs.mainIdea: All the things they were proud of — the candles, the books, the theater dreams — were left behind in Copenhagen.
paragraphs.simple: They had to leave everything behind: the candlesticks, the books, the theater dreams. Now they have only warm clothes, food, and the dark path to freedom.

paragraphs.context: But their shoulders were as straight as they had been in the past
paragraphs.mainIdea: Though they lost everything, they still stand tall, so they must carry another kind of pride inside that they did not leave behind.
paragraphs.simple: Their backs are as straight as they were in the classroom, on the stage, and at the Sabbath table. Their true pride is still with them.

paragraphs.context: she traced their route in her mind
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alone in the chair, Annemarie pictures the old path in her mind and walks with them in thought, remembering its turns and twisted trees.
paragraphs.simple: She sits and follows their way in her head. She knows the path too, with its turns, the trees with knotted roots, and the bushes that flower in early summer.

paragraphs.context: It would take them, she thought, half an hour to reach the place
paragraphs.mainIdea: She guesses the slow walk will take half an hour, then Mama will leave the Rosens at the boat and hurry home alone.
paragraphs.simple: She thinks they will reach Henrik's boat in thirty minutes. Mama will stay only a minute for a last hug, then walk home fast by herself, knowing the way well.

paragraphs.context: He would be wishing he could have come
paragraphs.mainIdea: She thinks of Papa alone in Copenhagen, awake and afraid, watching the clock and waiting for news that everyone is safe.
paragraphs.simple: Papa could not come with them. He must live as always and go to work. Now he is awake, afraid for them, and hoping to hear they are safe.

paragraphs.context: It was only the first hint of a slightly lightening sky
paragraphs.mainIdea: The first pale light of morning appears in the east, and she pictures dawn moving across Sweden and then over Denmark.
paragraphs.simple: It is not morning yet. There is only a pale gleam at the edge of the meadow. Far away, morning will soon come to Sweden, then to little Denmark.

paragraphs.context: something unfamiliar, something that had not been there the day before
paragraphs.mainIdea: At the start of the path she sees a dark, blurred heap. She forces herself to understand: it is her mother, lying on the ground.
paragraphs.simple: She looks out the window and sees a strange dark shape by the path. It moves. She knows with fear that it is Mama, lying on the earth.

paragraphs.context: he took them aboard and down below so quickly
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mama reports that Henrik was waiting and hid the Rosens below in the boat's cabin so fast that they seemed to vanish.
paragraphs.simple: She tells Annemarie they got there fast. Henrik was waiting on the boat. He took the Rosens down to the cabin so quickly that they were invisible in an instant.

paragraphs.context: you must pretend to be nothing more than a little girl
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mama warns her: if soldiers stop her, she must act like a silly little girl bringing lunch to her forgetful uncle.
paragraphs.simple: She must pretend to be a foolish, empty-headed child. If asked, she will say her uncle the fisherman forgot his lunch, and she is taking it to him.

paragraphs.context: entering the woods on the footpath, did Annemarie realize how cold the dawn was
paragraphs.mainIdea: Now on the dark path, Annemarie feels how cold the morning is. She wears only a light sweater over her dress.
paragraphs.simple: Earlier she watched the others put on warm coats. She has only a thin sweater. The October morning is gray, chilly, and damp, and she shivers.

paragraphs.context: "Once upon a time there was a little girl," she told herself silently
paragraphs.mainIdea: To comfort herself in the dark woods, Annemarie silently tells herself the story of Little Red Riding Hood that she used to tell Kirsti.
paragraphs.simple: She remembers the story she often told Kirsti in bed at night. Now, alone on the dark path, she tells it to herself to feel less afraid.

paragraphs.context: If she turned to the left, it would take her to the road
paragraphs.mainIdea: The left path leads to the road — lighter and wider, but more dangerous, with fishermen and perhaps soldiers. She turns right, deeper into the woods.
paragraphs.simple: She knows the turning well. The road would be brighter, but someone could see her there. Fishermen and soldiers may be about. So she goes right.

paragraphs.context: The local doctor was an old man, brusque and businesslike, though with kind eyes.
paragraphs.mainIdea: She thinks of the local doctor — rough and businesslike, but kind — who has helped the family in past summers.
paragraphs.simple: She hopes Mama has called the doctor. He is an old man who speaks shortly but has kind eyes. He came when baby Kirsti had an earache and when Lise burned her hand.

paragraphs.context: Then they were there, in front of her. Four armed soldiers.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Four armed soldiers with two big dogs step out in front of her on the path.
paragraphs.simple: Four soldiers with guns stand in front of her. With them are two large dogs, pulling hard at tight leashes, their eyes shining and their lips curled back.

paragraphs.context: But Annemarie knew that these woods were not like the woods in the story.
paragraphs.mainIdea: She knows these real woods hold no wolves or tigers — only the beasts of Kirsti's imagination.
paragraphs.simple: She hears a small noise and smiles. These woods are not like the story's woods. There are no wolves, bears, or tigers here, only in Kirsti's lively imagination.

paragraphs.context: a silly little girl, angered because the soldier had touched her hair
paragraphs.mainIdea: Kirsti was not frightened that day; she was just an angry little girl, and her childish anger amused the soldier.
paragraphs.simple: When soldiers stopped them before, Kirsti felt no fear. She was only angry because a soldier touched her hair. Knowing nothing of danger, she acted like a silly child, and the soldier laughed.

paragraphs.context: "Uncle Henrik doesn't even like fish," she said, laughing.
paragraphs.mainIdea: She chatters on like Kirsti, saying Henrik never eats fish because he sees and smells too much of it.
paragraphs.simple: She tries to giggle like her sister. She says Uncle Henrik does not like fish at all. He says he sees too much of it and smells too much of it.

paragraphs.context: Please, please, she implored in her mind. Don't lift the napkin.
paragraphs.mainIdea: She silently begs the soldier not to lift the napkin, which hides the packet.
paragraphs.simple: The soldier is looking at the basket's bottom. She fears he will lift the napkin and find what is under it. In her head she pleads with him not to do it.

paragraphs.context: The soldier took out the packet. "Why was this so carefully hidden?" he snapped.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The soldier finds the packet and demands why it was hidden. Annemarie says she does not know what it is — which is true.
paragraphs.simple: He pulls the packet from the basket and snaps at her. She cries that she does not know what it is. She truly has no idea what is inside.

paragraphs.context: "Your stupid mother has sent your uncle a handkerchief.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The soldier opens the packet, finds only a white handkerchief, and laughs at Danish women for hemming cloth for their men.
paragraphs.simple: He tears the paper open and looks inside. He sees just a folded white cloth. He calls Annemarie an idiot girl and says German women have better things to do.

paragraphs.context: She could see the look of relief on his face
paragraphs.mainIdea: Henrik glances into the basket and looks relieved: the packet is there, even though it was torn open.
paragraphs.simple: She sees his worried face change. He is glad the packet is still in the basket. His voice shows relief, and he thanks her.

paragraphs.context: That's all that brave means—not thinking about the dangers.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Uncle Henrik tells Annemarie what being brave really means.
paragraphs.simple: Being brave does not mean you feel no fear. It means you do not think about the danger. You only think about what you must do.

paragraphs.context: Many of the fishermen have built hidden places in their boats.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Henrik explains how fishermen hide people in secret places under their boats.
paragraphs.simple: Many fishermen have made secret hiding places inside their boats, under the floor. Peter and others in the Resistance bring people to them, and helpers along the way hide them too.

paragraphs.context: They are searching all the boats now.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Soldiers are searching every boat for escaping Jews, but they rarely find them.
paragraphs.simple: Many soldiers are searching all the boats along the coast. They know the Jews are escaping, but they rarely find them. The hiding places are carefully hidden, and dead fish on the deck keep the soldiers from looking closely.

paragraphs.context: it ruins their sense of smell.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The drug in the handkerchief attracts the dogs but destroys their sense of smell.
paragraphs.simple: Scientists made a special drug and put it in the handkerchief. It attracts the dogs, but when they sniff it, it ruins their sense of smell. Then the dogs cannot find the hidden people.

paragraphs.context: All of the ifs whirled in Annemarie's head.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annemarie thinks of all the bad things that could have happened.
paragraphs.simple: What if she had not found the packet? What if the soldiers had taken the basket? What if she had not reached the boat in time? All these worried thoughts spun quickly in her head.

paragraphs.context: Dark, and cold, and very cramped.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The hiding place was dark, cold, and very small, but the Rosens were brave.
paragraphs.simple: Under the boat it was dark, cold, and very small. Mrs. Rosen felt sick from the sea. But the Rosens were brave people. When they stepped onto land in Sweden, the air was fresh and cool.

paragraphs.context: The God of Thunder has fallen into the milk pail!
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annemarie laughs and points: the kitten, called the God of Thunder, has fallen into the milk pail.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie laughs and points at the pail of milk. The little kitten, called the God of Thunder, has fallen right into the milk!

paragraphs.context: neighbors had tended the plants and dusted the furniture
paragraphs.mainIdea: Neighbors cared for the empty apartments of the Jews who had fled; Mama did this for the Rosens.
paragraphs.simple: Many Jewish families had fled Denmark. For almost two years, neighbors took care of their empty apartments. They watered the plants and cleaned the furniture. Annemarie's mother did this for the Rosens.

paragraphs.context: It was a painful fact to recall on this day
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annemarie remembers that Peter was captured and executed by the Germans in a public square.
paragraphs.simple: Peter Neilsen was dead. On this happy day, it was painful to remember. The Germans had caught him and shot him in a public square in Copenhagen.

paragraphs.context: He had written a letter to them from prison
paragraphs.mainIdea: In his last letter, Peter said he loved them, was not afraid, and was proud of his work.
paragraphs.simple: The night before he died, Peter wrote from prison. He loved them and was not afraid. He was proud of his work for his country. He asked to be buried beside Lise.

paragraphs.context: they had laid flowers there, on the bleak, numbered ground.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They laid flowers on the numbered graves, and her parents told her the truth about Lise's death.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie and her parents laid flowers on the cold, numbered ground. That night, her parents told her the true story of how Lise died at the start of the war.

paragraphs.context: they raided the place that evening.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lise was at a secret meeting in a cellar when the Nazis raided it.
paragraphs.simple: Lise was with Peter and others in a cellar, holding secret meetings to make plans. The Nazis found out and raided the place that evening. They all ran in different directions, trying to escape.

paragraphs.context: people were dancing. It brought back another memory, the memory of Lise
paragraphs.mainIdea: The dancing reminded Annemarie of Lise in her yellow dress, dancing with Peter when they announced their engagement.
paragraphs.simple: People were dancing in the street. This brought back a memory. Long ago, Lise wore a yellow dress and danced with Peter on the night they told everyone they would marry.

paragraphs.context: Denmark surrendered to Germany in 1940, it is true
paragraphs.mainIdea: Denmark surrendered in 1940 because it was small and undefended; Germans then occupied it for five years.
paragraphs.simple: Denmark was small and had almost no army, so it surrendered to Germany in 1940. For five years, German soldiers occupied the country. They controlled the newspapers, trains, government, schools, and daily life.

paragraphs.context: the cocaine numbed their noses and destroyed, temporarily, their sense of smell.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The handkerchief is true: a powder that drew the dogs in but destroyed their sense of smell.
paragraphs.simple: Swedish scientists made a powder from dried rabbit's blood and cocaine. The blood attracted the dogs, but when they sniffed it, the cocaine numbed their noses and destroyed their sense of smell. Many lives were saved.

paragraphs.context: you must not dream yourselves back to the times before the war
paragraphs.mainIdea: In his last letter, he asked people to dream of a decent world, not of the past.
paragraphs.simple: The night before he died, he wrote to his mother. Do not dream of going back to before the war. Instead, dream of creating a world where all people treat each other with decency.

sentences.context: not a day goes by that I don't hear
sentences.grammar: 'Not a day goes by that I don't...' is a double negative meaning 'every day'; the two negatives cancel out to a positive.
sentences.simple: Not a single day passes without a passionate reader writing to me about the book.

sentences.context: Peter Neilsen brought it to them occasionally, carefully folded
sentences.grammar: Two main clauses joined by a semicolon; the dashes translate the Danish name, and 'carefully folded and hidden' are shortened passive phrases describing the newspaper.
sentences.simple: Peter secretly brought the banned newspaper, hidden among ordinary papers, and Mama burned it after reading.

sentences.context: the soldiers were simply part of the landscape, something that
sentences.grammar: 'Something that had always been there...' renames 'part of the landscape'; the long tail of phrases all describe the soldiers.
sentences.simple: To little Kirsti, the soldiers were just a normal part of everyday life, like lampposts.

sentences.context: He was not like fairy tale kings, who seemed
sentences.grammar: Two 'who'-clauses in parallel describe fairy-tale kings; the -ing forms ('giving', 'demanding', 'looking') shorten longer relative clauses.
sentences.simple: He was not like fairy-tale kings, who gave orders from balconies or sat on thrones finding husbands for their daughters.

sentences.context: In the blue carved trunk in the corner of
sentences.grammar: The verb 'were folded' comes before its subject (the pillowcases, dresses) because the long place-phrase opens the sentence — inverted word order.
sentences.simple: Lise's pillowcases, her unworn wedding dress, and her yellow dress lay folded in the blue trunk in the bedroom corner.

sentences.context: fearful that she had said the wrong thing, the
sentences.grammar: 'The thing that would bring...' repeats and explains 'the wrong thing' — an appositive phrase renaming what came before.
sentences.simple: Then she stopped, afraid she had said something wrong that would make her mother look sad.

sentences.context: Though his visits were always hurried—they almost seemed secret,
sentences.grammar: 'Though... still...' sets up a contrast: the first half admits the visits were rushed and secret, the second says she loved them anyway.
sentences.simple: His visits were always quick and almost secret, but seeing Peter was still a joy.

sentences.context: Then, suddenly, she sat upright, her eyes wide.
sentences.grammar: 'Her eyes wide' is a shortened clause with no verb ('her eyes [were] wide') describing her as she sat up.
sentences.simple: Then, suddenly, she sat up straight with her eyes open wide.

sentences.context: standing over there are two girls just our age, looking across
sentences.simple: Maybe two girls our age are standing over there, looking back and saying 'That is Denmark!'
sentences.grammar: Locative inversion: the place phrase 'standing over there' comes first, so the verb 'are' comes before the subject 'two girls'.

sentences.context: in all the stories I've heard, in all the old
sentences.simple: In all the stories and pictures, there was never any Great-aunt Birte.
sentences.grammar: Negative inversion: the negative opener 'Never once' flips the word order to 'has there been' instead of 'there has been'.

sentences.context: From the living room came the sound of a sleepy
sentences.simple: The sound of a sleepy baby crying briefly came from the living room.
sentences.grammar: Locative inversion: the place phrase 'From the living room' comes first, so the verb 'came' comes before the subject 'the sound'.

sentences.context: frightened the day—not long ago, though now it seemed far
sentences.simple: She had been very frightened on that day, when the soldier stopped her and asked questions.
sentences.grammar: Parenthetical dashes: the aside 'not long ago, though now it seemed far in the past' is tucked inside the main clause without breaking it.

sentences.context: It is Great-aunt Birte, who never was.
sentences.simple: It is Great-aunt Birte, who never really existed.
sentences.grammar: Ellipsis: 'who never was' drops the rest — it means 'who never lived' or 'who never existed'.

sentences.context: Although she didn't understand what was happening, or why the
sentences.simple: She did not understand the secret, but she knew it was safer for Ellen to believe the lie.
sentences.grammar: Concessive buildup: 'Although' opens a long list of things she did not understand before the main point 'she knew' arrives.

sentences.context: to picture the tall, aging king, perhaps with tears in
sentences.simple: Thinking of the old king looking at his ruined ships made her feel sad and proud too.
sentences.grammar: Causative 'make': 'made Annemarie feel' is followed by the long 'to picture...' phrase that names what she imagined.

sentences.context: suddenly the specter of guns and grim-faced soldiers seemed nothing
sentences.simple: At that happy moment, the real soldiers felt like only a scary story.
sentences.grammar: Delayed main clause: a long chain of scene details ('with cream...', 'and out in the Kattegat...') holds back the main verb 'seemed' until the end.

sentences.context: the night would be not only dark but very long
sentences.simple: The night was still light, but in winter it would be dark and very long.
sentences.grammar: 'Not only... but' pairs two adjectives ('dark', 'very long'); the tail phrase 'night skies beginning...' adds extra detail.

sentences.context: To be brave came more easily if you knew nothing.
sentences.grammar: The infinitive phrase 'To be brave' works as the subject of the verb 'came'.
sentences.simple: It is easier to be brave when you do not know how much danger there is.

sentences.context: The sky was, too, thought Annemarie.
sentences.grammar: The words 'too cold, too big' are left out because the last line just said them; 'thought Annemarie' sits in the middle of her own thought.
sentences.simple: Annemarie thought the sky was too cold and too big, too.

sentences.context: it was as if Ellen had moved now into a different world
sentences.grammar: 'as if' introduces something felt but not literally true: Ellen only seems to live in another world now.
sentences.simple: It felt like Ellen had moved into a different world.

sentences.context: It was one more time, Annemarie realized, when they protected one another
sentences.grammar: 'It was one more time ... when' marks this as another example of the same pattern; 'Annemarie realized' is just a tag in the middle.
sentences.simple: Once again, they kept each other safe by not telling dangerous things.

sentences.context: he had moved beyond his own youth and had taken his place
sentences.grammar: 'had moved' and 'had taken' are past perfect: they happened before the story's 'now'; 'as if' marks it as her feeling, not a fact.
sentences.simple: He had left his young days behind and now stood with the grown-ups.

sentences.context: her hair neatly combed and covered, lighting the Sabbath candles, saying the ancient prayer
sentences.grammar: 'her hair neatly combed and covered' has no verb of its own; it is an absolute phrase that describes Mrs. Rosen.
sentences.simple: She pictured Mrs. Rosen, hair neatly covered, lighting the Sabbath candles and praying.

sentences.context: trees whose gnarled roots pushed the earth now and then into knotted clumps
sentences.grammar: 'whose' joins the roots to the trees, like 'of the trees'; the clause picks out which trees she means.
sentences.simple: She remembered the twisted trees with their knotted roots pushing up the earth.

sentences.context: pausing a minute, no more, for a final hug
sentences.grammar: The dashes tuck a quick side detail into the sentence; 'no more' means 'not longer than that'.
sentences.simple: Mama would stop for only one short last hug, then turn and come home.

sentences.context: Dawn would creep across the Swedish farmland and coast
sentences.grammar: Dawn is given human actions ('creep', 'wash'); the two halves of the picture join with a semicolon.
sentences.simple: Morning light would slowly move across the Swedish land, then over Denmark.

sentences.context: forcing her eyes to understand, needing to understand, not wanting to understand
sentences.grammar: Three -ing phrases pile up to show her fear and her fight to face what she sees.
sentences.simple: She forced herself to see, though part of her did not want to.

sentences.context: something unfamiliar, something that had not been there the day before
sentences.grammar: The second 'something' explains the first; 'that had not been there' is a relative clause describing the shape.
sentences.simple: She saw a strange shape that had not been there yesterday.

sentences.context: I was very nearly here—well, maybe just halfway—when I tripped over a root
sentences.grammar: 'well, maybe just halfway' corrects herself inside dashes; 'very nearly here' means 'almost home'.
sentences.simple: I was almost home, or maybe only halfway, when a root tripped me.

sentences.context: "It's important, isn't it, Mama? It was for Uncle Henrik.
sentences.grammar: The short question 'isn't it' after a statement asks Mama to agree with her.
sentences.simple: This packet is important, isn't it, Mama? It was meant for Uncle Henrik.

sentences.context: It was the packet that Peter had given to Mr. Rosen.
sentences.grammar: 'It was X that ...' points at the thing and stresses exactly which one it is.
sentences.simple: It was the same packet Peter had given to Mr. Rosen.

sentences.context: the path, latticed with thick roots hidden under the fallen leaves, was invisible
sentences.grammar: The commas hold a long description between 'path' and its verb 'was invisible'; 'latticed' means crossed like a net.
sentences.simple: The path was hidden under thick roots and fallen leaves, so she could not see it.

sentences.context: none of the beasts that populated Kirsti's vivid imagination
sentences.grammar: 'none of the beasts' repeats 'no wolves or bears or tigers' in other words; 'that populated' tells which beasts.
sentences.simple: The scary animals from Kirsti's imagination did not live in these woods.

sentences.context: so that Kirsti, listening, would snuggle closer and wrap her arms around Annemarie
sentences.grammar: 'listening' sits between commas to remind us Kirsti is hearing the tale; 'so that' shows the result.
sentences.simple: On dark evenings in the story, Kirsti would hold Annemarie tight.

sentences.context: Annemarie willed herself, with all her being, to behave as Kirsti would.
sentences.grammar: 'with all her being' sits between commas to mean 'with everything in her'; 'would' stands in for 'would behave'.
sentences.simple: Annemarie forced herself to act just as Kirsti would.

sentences.context: as if he were going to return it to the basket
sentences.grammar: 'as if he were' pictures something untrue; 'were' (not 'was') marks it as imagined.
sentences.simple: He acted like he would put the cheese back, but he did not.

sentences.context: It wasn't hidden, any more than the napkin was
sentences.grammar: 'any more than X was' compares the two things: the packet was as open as the napkin.
sentences.simple: The packet was no more hidden than the napkin was.

sentences.context: she had run along the road to avoid the soldiers
sentences.grammar: Two em dashes mark a long interruption mid-sentence; the main clause — Mama and Kirsti were gone — comes only at the end.
sentences.simple: Annemarie ran home along the road to avoid soldiers. Carrying nothing, she was safe, but Mama and Kirsti were gone.

sentences.context: Wasn't that a nice surprise, that the Rosens came last night
sentences.grammar: A rhetorical question; the 'that'-clause after the comma names what the surprise was.
sentences.simple: The Rosens came last night to take Ellen home. Wasn't that a nice surprise?

sentences.context: the soldiers are so angry about the escaping Jews
sentences.grammar: 'So angry...that...': the anger is so great that it leads to a result — using trained dogs.
sentences.simple: The soldiers are angry because the Jews are escaping and they cannot find them. Now they use trained dogs.

sentences.context: we will each have such a handkerchief, each boat captain
sentences.grammar: 'Each boat captain' is an appositive: it restates and explains who 'we' means.
sentences.simple: Thanks to Peter, every boat captain will have one of these handkerchiefs.

sentences.context: If she had not found the packet where Mr. Rosen
sentences.grammar: A string of 'if' clauses with no main clause; the terrible result is left unsaid for the reader to imagine.
sentences.simple: What if she had not found the packet that Mr. Rosen dropped?

sentences.context: no longer was she a lighthearted chatterbox of a child
sentences.grammar: Inversion after the negative opener 'no longer': the verb 'was' comes before the subject 'she'.
sentences.simple: She was no longer a happy, talkative little child.

sentences.context: how devastating the day was when they received the news
sentences.grammar: A chain of noun clauses — 'how...was' holding 'when they received the news that...' — packs several facts into one object.
sentences.simple: Annemarie forced herself to think of Peter. The news of his death made the happy day feel terrible.

sentences.context: wanted to know it all, but wasn't certain that
sentences.grammar: Ellipsis: the subject 'she' is dropped before 'wasn't certain', borrowed from the first clause.
sentences.simple: She wanted to know everything, but she was not sure she could bear the painful truth.

sentences.context: So—surely with great sorrow—King Christian surrendered
sentences.grammar: Em dashes set off an authorial aside ('surely with great sorrow'); 'overnight' works as an adverb of sudden time.
sentences.simple: So the king surrendered, surely with great sadness, and the soldiers moved in overnight.

sentences.context: must be to create an ideal of human decency
sentences.grammar: 'One' stands in for 'an ideal'; 'narrow-minded and prejudiced' describe the kind of ideal he rejects.
sentences.simple: Instead, everyone must dream of building a world where people treat each other decently.
